BARRIERS: There are a number of barriers or issues that can get between people and enrolling and voting - which of these apply?
EXAMPLES: Examples

BARRIERS: Working or child care gets in the way
SPECIFIC ISSUES: Working or child care gets in the way of voting

EXAMPLES: I am a parent with young children and I have no one to watch them while I vote. Am I allowed to bring my children with me when I vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have to bring my kids with me
ANSWER: Vote – The law requires a person to enter the voting booth alone, which is intended to protect the secrecy of their vote. However, in practice, voters may take their children into the voting booth with them if they cannot be left unattended.

EXAMPLES: I'm an essential worker who is working on election day, can I leave work to vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am an essential worker / working on election day
ANSWER:
Vote – You are legally entitled to time away from work to vote on election day. You can also vote early at an [[advance-voting]] place. If you have not had a reasonable opportunity to vote before starting work on election day, and you are not required to carry out essential work or services, your employer must allow you to leave work to vote by 3pm. You are entitled to remain away from work for the rest of the day if necessary to vote, and your employer cannot deduct pay for this time. 

If you are required to work after 3pm to carry out essential work or services, your employer must allow you a reasonable amount of time earlier in the day to vote. Your employer cannot deduct pay for this time, provided you do not take more than two hours off work.

EXAMPLES: I am doing seasonal farming work during the election period. Can I still vote away from my usual address?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am living somewhere temporarily for work e.g. seasonal workers, sharemilkers, away at training
ANSWER:
Enrol – You can enrol online or by completing a paper form. Your residential address for enrolment purposes does not change if you are temporarily away from your usual home.

Vote – If you are away from your usual place of residence, you can vote at the nearest voting place. As your name will not appear on the printed electoral roll at that location, you will need to complete a special declaration vote form before voting. This is known as a [[special-vote]].
Source?: Electoral Act s 61(b), s 72(6)(a), and s 162.

EXAMPLES: I work night shifts and sleep during the day, how can I cast my vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am a shift worker
ANSWER: Vote – You can either vote during the [[advance-voting]] period or cast a [[takeaway-vote]].

BARRIERS: I can't physically get to a polling place
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I can't physically get to a polling place

EXAMPLES: I have to get surgery on the Friday before polling day, how do I vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I will be in hospital
ANSWER:
Enrol – You can enrol online or by completing a paper form, and you can have someone support you with the process if needed. Your enrolment address should be your usual residential address, not the hospital where you will be staying.

Vote – If you cannot get to a voting place because you are in hospital, you can authorise a friend or family member to collect your voting papers and bring them to you so you can cast a [[takeaway-vote]]. If you are scheduled to go into hospital before election day, it is best to vote in advance if you can. [[Advance-voting]] begins on **26 October**, 12 days before election day.

EXAMPLES: I have health issues and do not like being in public, crowded spaces. Can I still vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I can't leave care/ or the house
ANSWER: Vote – You can authorise someone to collect your voting papers from a voting place on your behalf - this process is known as a [[takeaway-vote]]. If you cannot get to a voting place and do not have someone who can collect your voting papers for you, contact your electorate manager. It may be possible for your voting papers to be delivered to you and then collected once you have completed them.

EXAMPLES: I am serving a 6 month home detention sentence, can I still enrol to vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am serving home detention
ANSWER:
Enrol – If you are on home detention, you can still enrol to vote, provided you meet the general eligibility criteria. You can enrol online or by completing a paper form.

Vote – You can vote if you are on home detention or serving a community-based sentence. Election officials will provide your local Probation Services office with information about the voting options available to you.

EXAMPLES: I live in a residential care facility and can't enrol or vote on my own, I have no family to help me with this, how can I vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am in a rest home
ANSWER: Vote - If you are in a rest home and you won’t be able to go to a voting place, you don’t need to contact the Electoral Commission. Your local Electorate Manager will contact the manager of your care home to arrange voting services.

EXAMPLES: I have lost a lot of motor functions, including the use of my hands… can I vote? How do I seek assistance to vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have a physical disability
ANSWER:
Enrol – You can ask someone, such as a friend or family member, to support you in completing your enrolment form or to complete it on your behalf. A person who is enrolled to vote can complete and sign the form for you, and someone with power of attorney can also complete and sign it on your behalf. You can enrol online, or upload, email or post a completed form.

Vote – You can authorise someone to collect your voting papers from a voting place and bring them to you - this process is known as a [[takeaway-vote]]. If you cannot get to a voting place and do not have someone who can collect your voting papers, contact your electorate manager. It may be possible for your voting papers to be delivered to you and then collected once you have completed them. 

You can also cast your vote at an [[advance-voting]] place and bring a support person with you, including behind the voting screen if you would like.
Source?: https://vote.nz/enrolling/get-help-to-enrol/need-help-to-enrol?lang=en-NZ  & https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/need-help-to-vote & Electoral Act s 170, s 167(2A), and s 85.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: Names and Identity

EXAMPLES: I don't have a license, passport, or kiwi access card, can I still enrol and vote without any of these?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have no ID
ANSWER:
Enrol – To enrol online, you need a **New Zealand drivers licence**, **New Zealand passport**, or a **verified RealMe identity**. 

If you do not have any of these, you can still enrol by completing an enrolment form online and having it emailed to you to sign, then uploading, emailing or posting the completed form. Alternatively, you can print a form yourself or request one to be sent to you, then return it by upload, email or post. 
Printed enrolment forms may also be available at selected public libraries, Electoral Commission offices, and potentially local post offices. Contact your local library or post office for more information.

Vote – You do not need to bring any form of ID to vote. Simply turn up at a voting place. You can bring your EasyVote card to make the process quicker, but if you do not have one, that is okay too. Your details can be confirmed at the voting place.

EXAMPLES: My prefered name differs from my legal name, and has not been legally changed from my birth name. I am concerned about being questioned in public when I go to vote.
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am gender diverse and have changed my name
ANSWER:
Enrol – While the Electoral Act requires your 'full' name to be used for voting and enrolment purposes, the Electoral Comissions does allow preferred names to be used (this does not have to match a legal record). 

If you are already enrolled but would like to change your enrolment details to match your preferred name, and this name vastly differs from the name that your are currently enrolled under, please ensure that you include this name when you are updating your details e.g., (previously enrolled as *Full name*) - this is to avoid potential issues regarding duplicate records. 

Please note, you may be limited when trying to use the online enrolment service, as it uses the details from your New Zealand passport, drivers licence or verified RealMe identity. If your preferred name does not match these records, you may need to complete a paper enrolment form instead and then upload, email or post it to the Electoral Commission. You may be contacted by the Electoral Comission to double check these details.

Vote – You can vote using your preferred name if you were able to update your details before the enrolment due date on **25 October**.

EXAMPLES: I no longer identify with my divorce husbands surname. Can I vote with my maiden name, despite not legally changing my name on my ID?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have made a change to my legal name e.g. through marriage, divorce, adoption, or reclaiming an ingoa Māori
ANSWER:
Enrol – While the Electoral Act requires your 'full' name to be used for voting and enrolment purposes, the Electoral Comissions does allow preferred names to be used (this does not have to match a legal record). 

If you are already enrolled but would like to change your enrolment details to match your preferred name, and this name vastly differs from the name that your are currently enrolled under, please ensure that you include this name when you are updating your details e.g., (previously enrolled as *Full name*) - this is to avoid potential issues regarding duplicate records. 

Please note, you may be limited when trying to use the online enrolment service, as it uses the details from your New Zealand passport, drivers licence or verified RealMe identity. If your preferred name does not match these records, you may need to complete a paper enrolment form instead and then upload, email or post it to the Electoral Commission. You may be contacted by the Electoral Comission to double check these details.

Vote – You can vote using your preferred name if you were able to update your details before the enrolment due date on **25 October**.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: Age

EXAMPLES: I am currently 17 years old and won't turn 18 until the day before election. Can I still enrol to vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am 17 but will turn 18 on or before the election day
ANSWER:
Enrol – You can complete an enrolment form when you are 17. On your 18th birthday, you will be automatically enrolled and able to vote.

Vote – If you turn 18 on election day, you can still vote as normal, provided you enrolled beforehand. If you enrolled **before 4 October**, you can cast an [[election-day-vote]]. If you enrolled **after 4 October but before 25 October**, you will cast a [[special-vote]] at the voting place.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: I don't have a normal, fixed address

EXAMPLES: I'll be in a remote area during the election with no voting places near me, how can I cast a vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I live in a remote area
ANSWER:
Vote – You can authorise someone to collect your voting papers from a voting place on your behalf. If you cannot get to a voting place and do not have someone who can collect your voting papers, contact your electorate manager. 

They may be able to arrange for your voting papers to be delivered to you and then collected once you have completed them. If you are in a remote location within Aotearoa New Zealand, you may also be able to cast a [[special-vote]] if voting at a polling place would not be practicable without causing hardship or serious inconvenience. 

If you are unable to reach a voting place because you are in a remote location—for example, on a remote island administered by the Department of Conservation, at an offshore installation, or working on a vessel during the voting period—the Electoral Commission has a separate process for arranging voting services. For more information, call 0800 36 76 56.

EXAMPLES: I work on a cruise ship and will be working away from port during election time, how can I enrol and vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I work at sea
ANSWER:
Enrol – Your residential address for enrolment purposes does not change if you are temporarily absent from it.

Vote – If you are working on a ship that is in port and you are enrolled, or eligible to enrol, in the electorate where the ship is located, your ship’s master must allow you to go ashore to vote. If the ship will not be in port, or will not return to port, during the voting period, you may be eligible for a [[special-vote]]. 

For help with enrolling and voting, contact the Electoral Commission closer to election time on 0800 36 76 56 or at <enquiries@elections.govt.nz>.
Source?: https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/cant-get-to-a-voting-place & Electoral Act Section 72(6)(a) and s 61(b) & https://vote.nz/contact-us

EXAMPLES: For the past few years, I have been living full-time on a boat. Can I enrol to vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I live on a boat
ANSWER: Enrol – If your home is on a ship or boat that is permanently moored in a harbour, use the address of the ship or boat as your residential address. If your home is on a travelling ship or boat, use the last New Zealand address where you lived for at least one month, even if this was some time ago. You will also need to provide a postal address where you can receive mail, such as a PO Box or the address of a friend, family member, church or support group.

EXAMPLES: I am experiencing homelessness/am unhoused and do no have an address to enrol, how can I still complete my enrolment form?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I do not have stable housing or a normal address
ANSWER:
Enrol – You can enrol at a place where you spend a lot of time, or use your last residential address where you lived for at least one month, even if this was some time ago. If you do not feel safe receiving mail at this address, you can provide a different *postal* address where you can safely receive correspondence, such as the address of a friend, family member, church or support group.

Vote – The Electoral Commission lists all voting places online, so you can find one near you, or you can call 0800 36 76 56 for assistance. Voting places are often located at community hubs. 

To vote, simply go to a voting place during the [[advance-voting]] period from **26 October to 6 October** or on election day on **7 October**. The voting team will support you through the process, and you do not need to bring any form of ID.

EXAMPLES: I am a kiwi who has recently moved overseas and do not have a New Zealand address, can I still vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I live overseas and do not have a New Zealand address
ANSWER:
Enrol – If you are a New Zealand citizen who has lived in New Zealand continuously for more than 12 months at some point in your life and have been in New Zealand within the last three years, you are still eligible to enrol to vote. 

Not having a current New Zealand address does not prevent you from enrolling. Your electorate will be based on the last New Zealand address where you lived for at least **one month**, and you can use your overseas address as your *postal* address to receive correspondence. 

You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport**, **New Zealand drivers licence** or **verified RealMe identity**. If you do not have any of these, you can enrol using a paper form.

Vote – If you are overseas, you can download your voting papers from the Electoral Commission’s website, complete them and upload them online (uou cannot return voting papers by email).

A link to download your voting papers will be available when overseas voting opens on **21 October**.You can complete the papers digitally or by hand. If completing them by hand, you can scan and upload them online, or post or hand-deliver them to an overseas voting place. 

If uploading your voting papers, they must be received by **7pm (NZ time)** on election day, which is **7 November**. 
You may also be able to vote in person at an overseas voting place. A list of overseas voting places will be available on the Electoral Commission’s website before the election.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: Enrolment issues

EXAMPLES: I haven't voted in a while. I have tried to enrol but found I have been placed on the dormant roll. How do I vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have been placed on the dormant roll
ANSWER:
Enrol – To come off the [dormant-roll], you simply need to update your enrolment address. You must do this before voting starts on **26 October 2026**, as you cannot update your enrolment at a voting place. To check or update your enrolment details, visit vote.nz or call 0800 36 76 56.

Vote – If you update your enrolment address before enrolment closes, you can vote normally. 

If you do not update your address **before midnight on 25 October** and have been on the dormant roll for less than three years, you can still vote. If your current address is in the same electorate as your previous enrolment address, you can cast both a party vote and an electorate vote. If your current address is in a different electorate, you can only cast a party vote.

EXAMPLES: I have moved address recently, how do I change my enrollment information?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: My enrolment details have changed
ANSWER: Enrol – You can enrol, check or update your details online at vote.nz using your **New Zealand drivers licence**, **New Zealand passport** or **verified RealMe identity**. You can also call 0800 36 76 56 to request an enrolment form, or free-text your name and address to 3676 to have a form sent to you. Providing your email address, phone number and postal address to the Electoral Commission will help them keep you updated about enrolment and voting.

EXAMPLES: I worry that my abusive ex partner will find my new confidential address if I enrol to vote. Can I enrol to vote without my information becoming publicly accessible?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I want to be on the unpublished roll
ANSWER:
Enrol – You can apply to be on the unpublished roll, which means your details will not appear on publicly available printed electoral rolls. 

To apply, you can download and complete an application form and email it to the Electoral Commission, or call 0800 36 76 56 to have a form sent to you by post. You will need to provide evidence explaining why you need to be on the unpublished roll, such as a letter from your employer, lawyer, social worker, advocate or another person of standing in the community explaining why your circumstances place you at risk. You can also provide documents such as a current protection order under the Family Violence Act 2018 or a restraining order under the Harassment Act 1997.

Vote – You can vote at any voting place in a general election, referendum or by-election. You will need to cast a [[special-vote]] because your details will not appear on the printed electoral roll used to issue voting papers at the voting place.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: Health and disability

EXAMPLES: I have to get surgery on the Friday before polling day, how do I vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I will be/am currently in the hospital
ANSWER:
Enrol – You can enrol online or by completing a paper form, and you can have someone support you with the process if needed. Your enrolment address should be your usual residential address, not the hospital where you will be staying.

Vote – If you cannot get to a voting place because you are in hospital, you can authorise a friend or family member to collect your voting papers and bring them to you so you can cast a [[takeaway-vote]]. If you are scheduled to go into hospital before election day, it is best to vote in advance if you can. [[Advance-voting]] begins on **26 October**, 12 days before election day.

EXAMPLES: I've been detained in a hospital or secure facility for more than 3 years, can I still enrol and vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am sectioned under the Mental Health Act
ANSWER:
Enrol - If you’ve been detained in a hospital or secure facility for 3 years or less, you can enrol and vote, as long as you meet the general eligibility requirements for enrolment.

If you’ve been detained in a hospital or secure facility, or you’re subject to a compulsory treatment order, for more than three years, under:

- Section 24, or section 31 or section 33 of the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act 2003, or under the corresponding provisions of the Criminal Justice Act 1985 (having been found unfit to stand trial or acquitted on account of insanity)
- Section 34 of the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act 2003 or section 118 of the Criminal Justice Act 1985 (following conviction for an offence)
- Section 45(2) of the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 (the Mental Health Act), or section 29(1) of the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 (for treatment of persons otherwise detained in prison because of their mental health or intellectual disability)

then you are *ineligible* to enrol and vote while you’re detained.

The Director of Mental Health (or their delegate) is required to inform the Electoral Commission of any person detained in a hospital or secure facility who is, or becomes, ineligible to vote. The Electoral Commission will then remove them from the electoral roll.

When a person detained in a hospital or secure facility has been transferred from a prison or is released from the facility (as long as they are not released to prison), the Director of Mental Health is required to provide them with the opportunity to enrol to vote, if they are eligible. If they choose to exercise that opportunity, the Director of Mental Health must pass their enrolment information to the Electoral Commission.

Vote - If you have been detained for 3 years or less as at election day you can enrol to vote if you also meet the general eligibility requirements. If you are eligible to vote from your facility, you’ll be able to participate in the 2026 General Election if you choose to. The Electoral Commission will work with your facility to provide you with voting services.

EXAMPLES: I am partially blind and need help reading and marking the paper to vote
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am blind or have low vision
ANSWER:
Enrol - A support person can help you enrol online or via paper form if you're blind or have low vision. If you can't sign the form, a support person can complete the form on your behalf. 

Vote - You may bring a support person to assist you that can help you vote, read out the voting paper and mark the paper for you if necessary. Furthermore, a telephone dictation voting service is available for blind and vision-impaired voters and voters who have a physical disability that prevents them from marking the voting paper independently and in secret. You need to register to use this service, even if you've used it at previous elections.

Registration for the telephone dictation service opens on Monday 5 October 2026, and will close at noon (NZT) on election day, Saturday 7 November 2026.

Voting with the telephone dictation service opens on Wednesday 21 October 2026, and will close at 7pm (NZT) on election day, Saturday 7 November 2026.

EXAMPLES: I have lost a lot of motor functions, including the use of my hands… can I vote? How do I seek assistance to vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have a physical disability
ANSWER:
Enrol – You can ask someone, such as a friend or family member, to support you in completing your enrolment form or to complete it on your behalf. A person who is enrolled to vote can complete and sign the form for you, and someone with power of attorney can also complete and sign it on your behalf. You can enrol online, or upload, email or post a completed form.

Vote – You can authorise someone to collect your voting papers from a voting place and bring them to you. This is known as a [[takeaway-vote]]. 

If you cannot get to a voting place and do not have someone who can collect your voting papers, contact your electorate manager. It may be possible for your voting papers to be delivered to you and then collected once you have completed them. 

You can also cast a vote in the [[advance-voting]] period and bring a support person with you to the voting place, including behind the voting screen if you would like.
Source?: https://vote.nz/enrolling/get-help-to-enrol/need-help-to-enrol?lang=en-NZ  & https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/need-help-to-vote & Electoral Act s 170, s 167(2A), and s 85.

EXAMPLES: I struggle with severe anxiety and don't know if I can vote on my own, how can I get help to enrol and vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have a mental health issue
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can ask a support person to help you enrol online if you wish. A support person can also complete and sign an enrolment form on your behalf if you require help because of a mental impairment. To *sign* the enrolment form on your behalf, the support person must be enrolled to vote; have enduring power of attorney; or be the person’s appointed welfare guardian. If required, the support person can also fill in another form so we can contact them as your representative.

Vote - If you need help with voting, a friend, family member or electoral official can be your support person and assist you.

Your support person can:

- Go behind the voting screen with you
- Read out the words and information on your voting paper
- Mark the voting papers for you if you ask them to.
- Your support person can't tell you who you should vote for. 

You can vote as long as you want to and can clearly indicate your voting choice. However, you must be present and able to indicate you choice at the time the vote is cast. If you're not able to do this, no one can cast a vote on your behalf, even someone with power of attorney or guardianship.

EXAMPLES: My grandparent has dementia, can they still vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have dementia or am helping someone with dementia
ANSWER:
Enrol - A support person can help someone with dementia to enrol to vote. A support person can also complete and sign an enrolment form on their behalf if they require help. 

To *sign* the enrolment form on their behalf, the support person must be enrolled to vote; have enduring power of attorney; or be the person’s appointed welfare guardian. If you're helping someone with dementia enrol, you will need to fill in another form so we can contact you as their representative. Ring 0800 36 76 56 for the form.

Vote - People living with dementia, or any other cognitive impairment, are able to continue to vote if they wish to do so. They can have help voting by taking a support person with them to the voting place.

A person with dementia can vote as long as they want to and can clearly indicate their voting choice. However, they must be present and able to indicate their choice at the time the vote is cast. If they're not able to do this, no one can cast a vote on their behalf, even someone with power of attorney or guardianship.

EXAMPLES: I struggle with gripping pens/pencils to write and need help marking the voting papers
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I need help marking the paper
ANSWER: Vote - You may bring a support person to assist you, they can help you vote, read out the voting paper and mark the paper for you if necessary. Your support person cannot tell you who to vote for.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: Prison, Remand, Home Detention etc

EXAMPLES: I am serving a 6 month home detention sentence, how can I my vote if I can't leave home?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am on home detention
ANSWER:
Enrol – If you are on home detention, you can still enrol to vote, provided you meet the general eligibility criteria. You can enrol online or by completing a paper form.

Vote – You can vote if you are on home detention or serving a community-based sentence. Election officials will provide your local Probation Services office with information about the voting options available to you.

EXAMPLES: I am currently serving a prison sentence of 2 years, can I still vote and will I be able to vote from prison?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am in prison
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can still enrol, but this depends on when the offences you were sentenced for occured. If the offences you were sentenced for were before 20 December 2025 and your sentence is under 3 years, you can enrol and vote. Prison staff assist those who are eligible and enrolment applications are individually scanned and emailed to the Electoral Commission.

Voting - This depends on when the offences you were sentenced for occured. If the offences you were sentenced for were before 20 December 2025 and your sentence is under 3 years, you can vote. During the [[advance-voting]] period, mobile voting teams will attend prisons and set up voting facilities for prisoners who are eligible to vote.

EXAMPLES: I'm in prison while on remand waiting for my trial, can I still enrol to vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am on remand
ANSWER:
Enrol - If you're on remand, you can still enrol to vote if you meet the general eligibility criteria. You do not face the same restrictions as those who have been sentenced. If you are in prison while on remand, prison staff will assist those who are eligible and enrolment applications are individually scanned and emailed to the Electoral Commission.

Vote - If you're in a police cell in the electorate on election day, a voting team may visit before midday so you can vote. If you are in prison while on remand, during the [[advance-voting]] period, mobile voting teams will attend prisons and set up voting facilities for those who are eligible to vote.

EXAMPLES: I'm serving a community service sentence can I still vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am on community service
ANSWER:
Enrol - If you're serving a community based sentence, you can still enrol to vote. You can do this online or via paper form.

Vote - You can vote if you're on home detention or serving a community-based sentence. Election officials will give your local Probation Services information about the voting options available to you.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: Overseas voters

EXAMPLES: I am living or staying in Australia at the time of the election, can I still enrol and vote and how can I do it?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am living overseas
ANSWER:
Enrol - If you are a New Zealand citizen, who has lived in New Zealand for more than 12 months continuously at some point in your life **AND** have been to New Zealand in the last 3 years - you are still eligible to enrol to vote. Your electorate will be where you last lived in New Zealand for longer than 1 month and you may set your postal address to your overseas address to ensure you receive correspondence. 

You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or a **New Zealand drivers licence** or a **verified Realme login**. If you don't have either of these, you can also enrol via paper form.

Vote - You can cast a [[special-vote]].
The best way to vote from overseas is to download your voting papers from the electoral commission's website, complete them, then upload them online (you cannot send back voting papers through email). 

A link to download your voting papers will be available on the electoral commission's website from the date overseas voting opens on **21 October**. You can complete the papers both digitally (marking the paper digitally) or physically, if you choose to complete them by hand you can scan and upload them online, or you can post or hand deliver them to your nearest overseas voting place. 

If you're uploading your voting papers, you must return them by **7pm (NZ time)** on election day which is **7 November**.

You may also be able to vote at an overseas voting place. A list of overseas voting places will be available on the electoral commission's website prior to the election.

EXAMPLES: I am a member of the New Zealand Defence Force and stationed overseas, can I still enrol to vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am overseas as a member of the military or diplomatic service
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can enrol and vote no matter how long you've been outside of New Zealand if you are one of the following: public servant working overseas and their families; New Zealand diplomats or trade representatives and their families; members of the New Zealand Defence Force and their families. 

You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or a **New Zealand drivers licence** or a **verified Realme login**. If you don't have either of these, you can also enrol via paper form.

Vote - You can cast a [[special-vote]].
The best way to vote from overseas is to download your voting papers from the electoral commission’s website, complete them, then upload them (you cannot send back voting papers through email). 

A link to download your voting papers will be available on the electoral commission's website from the date overseas voting opens on **21 October**. You can complete the papers both digitally or physically, if you choose to complete them by hand you can scan and upload them online, or you can post or hand deliver them to your nearest overseas voting place. 

If you're uploading your voting papers, you must return them by **7pm (NZ time)** on election day which is **7 November**.

EXAMPLES: I am living somewhere temporarily for work for a few months, how do I vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am a seasonal worker or temporarily living overseas for work
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can still enrol and vote if you are a New Zealand citizen or resident for electoral purposes and only residing outside of New Zealand temporarily for work (if you have been back to New Zealand in the last 3 years). Your residential address for enrolment purposes does not change because you are temporarily absent from it. 

You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or a **New Zealand drivers licence** or a **verified Realme login**. If you don't have either of these, you can also enrol via paper form.

Vote - You can cast a [[special-vote]].
The best way to vote from overseas is to download your voting papers from the electoral commission’s website, complete them, then upload them (you cannot send back voting papers through email). 

A link to download your voting papers will be available on the electoral commission's website from the date overseas voting opens on **21 October**. You can complete the papers both digitally or physically, if you choose to complete them by hand you can scan and upload them online, or you can post or hand deliver them to your nearest overseas voting place.

If you're uploading your voting papers, you must return them by **7pm (NZ time)** on election day which is **7 November**.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: Migrant in NZ, Residents & Language

EXAMPLES: I am a migrant in NZ who has been here for 2 years and I have never voted before, am I able to vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have migrated to New Zealand / I am a resident or visa holder
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can enrol to vote as a migrant, resident or visa holder **IF** you have a visa that does not require you to leave within a specified time **AND** you must have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more (this generally counts from your arrival to the country not from when you were granted your current visa). You do not have to be a permanent resident to enrol to vote. 

You also must not be subject to sections 15 or 16 of the Immigration Act, for example have a conviction for certain offenses.

Vote - You can cast a vote during the [[advance-voting]] period or cast an [[election-day-vote]].
Source?: https://vote.nz/enrolling/get-ready-to-enrol/are-you-eligible-to-enrol-and-vote Electoral Act s 74(1)(b) and s 73 & Immigration Act s 15 and s 16

EXAMPLES: Can I take someone in to help me vote if I don't speak English?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I need help with English
ANSWER:
Enrol - Enrolment information is available in several different languages and accessible formats to help guide you. The enrolment form itself is in English, if you require help with this you are able to ask someone around you for help to complete it.

Vote - You are allowed to take a support person into the voting booth to help you translate, read and/or mark the voting papers. This can be a friend, family member or you may ask an electoral official to help you. They can go behind the voting screen with you to help, but they may not instruct you on who to vote for.

EXAMPLES: I am an Australian citizen who has lived in New Zealand for 3 years, can I vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am an Australian citizen residing in New Zealand
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can enrol and vote once you have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more. You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or *New Zealand drivers licence* or a **verified Realme login**, if you do not have these, you can complete a paper form.

Vote - You can cast a vote during the [[advance-voting]] period or cast an [[election-day-vote]].

EXAMPLES: I am from Niue, Cook Islands or Tokelau and I don't know if I can enrol and vote in New Zealand
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am from the realm countries e.g. Niue, Cook Islands, or Tokelau
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can enrol and vote once you have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more. If you have not been to New Zealand for over 12 months you cannot vote. You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or **New Zealand drivers licence** or a **verified Realme login**, if you do not have these, you can complete a paper form.

Vote - You can cast a vote during the [[advance-voting]] period or cast an [[election-day-vote]]; or a [[special-vote]] (if you are not currently in NZ).

SPECIFIC ISSUES: Summary
ANSWER: Description

SPECIFIC ISSUES: A special vote is no different to a normal vote, except special voters must also sign a declaration form when they vote.
ANSWER:
A special vote is no different to a normal vote, except special voters must also sign a declaration form when they vote. There are several reasons why someone might need to cast a special vote. This includes if your name is not on the printed roll at a voting place by the time voting begins, this might occur because of the following reasons:

- You enrolled after the roll was printed (writ day **4 October**)
- You're voting away from your home electorate
- You're on the unpublished roll

When you get to a voting place, you'll need to fill out and sign a 'special declaration vote' form before you can vote, then you cast your vote as normal. 

Special votes are counted in the days following the election day. Special votes also include overseas votes, [[takeaway-vote]]s, and postal votes.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: A takeaway vote is for those who cannot physically make it to a voting place during the advance voting period or on election day.
ANSWER:
A takeaway vote is for those who cannot physically make it to a voting place during the advance voting period or on election day. For those who cannot make it to a voting place nearby, you can authorise someone else to pick up your voting papers for you and bring them to you.

Closer to the election you will be able to download a form from the electoral commission's website which you will sign and ask someone to take it to a voting place. They will then bring back your voting papers to complete.

If you're not able to download and print the form, you can write the following information by hand on a piece of paper and have someone take it to a voting place. The handwritten authorisation must include:

- Your first and last name
- Your contact phone number
- The address where you're enrolled to vote
- The electoral roll (general or Māori) you believe you are enrolled on
- A statement authorize the bearer to collect voting papers on your behalf.

If you are completing a takeaway vote, your voting papers must be returned to a voting place **before** voting closes at **7pm** on election day on **7 November**.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: The 7th of November is the official date of the 2026 general election. It is considered the formal voting date of the general election, votes cast on this date will be counted as a regular vote (subject to some special vote exceptions).
ANSWER:
The 7th of November is the official date of the 2026 general election. It is considered the formal voting date of the general election, votes cast on this date will be counted as a regular vote (subject to some special vote exceptions). 

On election day voting places must be open from 9am-7pm across New Zealand.

The voting places available near you will be posted by the electoral commission 3 weeks before election day. 

<https://map.vote.nz/voting-places> - Closer to the voting period this link will have information for you to check which voting place is near you.  

When you go to vote you can take your EasyVote card with you (you should receive this in the mail or via email). If you don't have a card or forget it, you can still vote.

When you arrive to vote, someone will be there to guide you and answer your questions. 

Give your EasyVote card to the person issuing voting papers or confirm your name and address to them. They’ll find your name on the electoral roll and give you a voting paper. Once you get your voting paper, you will be able to take it to a voting screen where you can vote privately.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: Advance voting begins 12 days before election day. This means in the 2026 election, any vote casted from the 26th of October until the 7th of November is an advance vote, and any vote made on the 7th of November is counted as an election day vote.
ANSWER:
Advance voting begins **12 days before** election day. This means in the 2026 election, any vote cast from the **26th of October** until the **6th of November** is an advance vote, and any vote made on the **7th of November** is counted as an [[election-day-vote]]. 

The process of advance voting is the same as an [[election-day-vote]], it just allows those who may be busy on election day or those who want to get in as early as possible, to cast their vote. 

There will be several advance voting places available to you in your electorate, you will be able to check where all the nearby voting places are and their hours on the electoral commission's website 3 weeks before election day.

<https://map.vote.nz/voting-places> - Closer to the voting period this link will have information for you to check which voting place is near you. 

When you go to vote you can take your EasyVote card with you (you should receive this in the mail or via email). If you don't have a card or forget it, you can still vote.

When you arrive to vote, someone will be there to guide you and answer your questions. 

Give your EasyVote card to the person issuing voting papers or confirm your name and address to them. They’ll find your name on the electoral roll and give you a voting paper. Once you get your voting paper, you will be able to take it to a voting screen where you can vote privately.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: The Māori Electoral Option is a choice for all those with Māori descent on which electoral roll to choose when voting.
ANSWER:
The Māori Electoral Option is a choice for all those of Māori descent on which electoral roll to choose when voting. 

Māori are able to choose to enrol on the Māori roll or the general roll, they can change this any time except 3 months before an election. This year the closing date to change rolls was **Midnight 6 August**, but if you are Māori and still haven't enrolled you can still choose which roll once you complete you enrolment, the last day to complete you enrolment is **25 October**.

Your roll choice affects which candidates you can choose to vote for in parliamentary elections **AND** local elections for you electorate vote in particular. If you choose the Māori roll, you will vote for a candidate in the Māori electorate you live in. If you choose the general roll, you will vote for a candidate in the general electorate you live in. The options when voting for a political party remains the same across both rolls. 

It is also important as it helps determine the number of Māori and general electorates - the number of Māori who are enrolled on the Māori roll could mean an increase in the number of electorates, a decrease, or it can stay the same for future elections. There are currently seven Māori electorates and 65 general electorates. 

In the future, if you wish to change your roll choice, you can do so easily online if you have a **New Zealand passport** or **New Zealand drivers license** or a **Realme verified login**. You can also update your choice via the paper form.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: Your address for the purpose of enrolment is the place you have most recently resided in for 1 month or longer.
ANSWER:
Your address for the purpose of enrolment is the place you have most recently resided in for 1 month or longer.

For those who may have unstable housing conditions, who frequently move, or are overseas, you may change your **postal** address to ensure you receive any correspondence from the electoral commision - but your **residential** address should remain the place you last resided in New Zealand for 1 month or longer.

If you have recently moved, but by the election date you will have lived in your current address for 1 month or longer, you may change your address to this in advance of the election date.

It is important for your address to be up to date, if it isn't, you may eventually be removed from the electoral roll. The electoral commission will attempt to text or email you before this happens.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: If the Electoral commission is unable to reach you via email, address, or phone,  you’ll be placed on the dormant roll. When you're on the dormant roll, you're still eligible to vote but won't appear on the printed roll at voting places.
ANSWER:
If the Electoral commission is unable to reach you via email, address, or phone, you’ll be placed on the dormant roll. 

When you're on the dormant roll, you're still eligible to vote but won't appear on the printed roll at voting places. This means you'll have to make a [[special-vote]]. If your new address is in a different electorate to your old address, it may also mean that only your party vote will count. Being on the dormant roll does not affect your roll type (general or Māori). 

Once you've been on the dormant roll for **3 years**, you will be **removed** from the electoral roll. The Electoral Comission is required to do this under the Electoral Act 1993. 

To come off the dormant roll you just need to update your address details – but be aware that you can't do this right before voting starts. To make sure you're removed from the dormant roll for the 2026 General Election, check and update your details before midnight, **Sunday 25 October 2026**. 

The only other circumstances where we remove someone from the electoral roll would be if they have passed away, if they have moved overseas, or if they have become ineligible for another reason such as being sentenced to a prison term.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: If you're concerned about your personal safety, or that of your family, you can apply to go on the confidential unpublished roll. The Electoral Commission will keep your enrolment details secure and we won't give them to anyone.
ANSWER:
If you're concerned about your personal safety, or that of your family, you can apply to go on the confidential unpublished roll. 

The Electoral Commission will keep your enrolment details secure and we won't give them to anyone. Going on the unpublished roll means your details won’t be included on printed electoral rolls. It also means you won't be able to check or update your enrolment details online. 

You'll need to make a [[special-vote]] at parliamentary and local elections. 

You need to provide information that shows why you need to register on the unpublished roll. Here are some examples of the type of information to include (you don't need all of these types of information to apply):

- A letter explaining why your work or personal circumstances place you at risk. This letter could be from your employer, lawyer, social worker, advocate, or someone of standing in the community. 
- A copy of a protection order that is in force under the Family Violence Act 2018. 
- A copy of a restraining order that is in force under the Harassment Act 1997. 
- Information from a police officer or corrections officer explaining why publishing your name and address could prejudice you or your family’s safety.
